title: Geometric semisimplicity, invariant complements and arbitrary field extension
statement: Let $k$ be a perfect field [def-weil-field], meaning every algebraic extension is separable, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $T:V\to V$ be $k$-linear. Let $m_T\in k[X]$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring] be the monic polynomial of least degree annihilating $T$, with $m_T=1$ when $V=0$. The following are equivalent: (i) every $T$-invariant subspace $U$ has a $T$-invariant complement $U'$ with $V=U\oplus U'$; (ii) $m_T$ is separable, meaning that its roots in an algebraic closure are distinct; (iii) $T$ is geometrically semisimple, meaning that its scalar extension to an algebraic closure of $k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] has a basis of eigenvectors. For every field extension $L/k$, not necessarily perfect or algebraic, let $T_L=1\otimes T$ on $L\otimes_k V$, where the tensor product is universal for $k$-bilinear maps and $T_L(\lambda\otimes v)=\lambda\otimes T(v)$. Then $T_L$ is geometrically semisimple if and only if $T$ is geometrically semisimple. Geometric semisimplicity over $L$ means diagonalizability after extension to an algebraic closure of $L$. All assertions include $V=0$.

proof.text: If $V=0$, then $L\otimes_k V=0$: every pure tensor is zero and pure tensors span by the tensor universal property. The only subspace has the zero complement, $m_T=1$ is separable, and the empty basis is an eigenbasis over every field. Thus all assertions hold. In the remaining argument zero spaces are still permitted; the products over no eigenvalues are $1$.

source.place: Section 9b, p.166: conventions for the zero vector space, supplied explicitly.

proof.text: First, the meaning of separability in (ii) agrees with the one in the cited nodes [def-pc-separable-polynomial], coprimality with the derivative; this holds for any field $K$ with an algebraic closure $\Omega$ and any monic $m\in K[X]$, in particular $m=m_T$. By [lem-weil-alg-closed-linear-factorization], $m=\prod_{j=1}^n(X-\gamma_j)$ in $\Omega[X]$ with leading coefficient $1$; the roots of $m$ in $\Omega$ are distinct exactly when no $(X-\gamma)^2$ with $\gamma\in\Omega$ divides $m$ in $\Omega[X]$, and then the $\gamma_j$ are pairwise distinct, since $\gamma_i=\gamma_j$ for $i\ne j$ gives such a square. In that case [lem-weil-pbc-distinct-linear-factors-separable], applied to $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $Q=m$, makes $m$ coprime to $m'$. Conversely, if $Um+Vm'=1$ with $U,V\in K[X]$ and $m=(X-\gamma)^2g$ in $\Omega[X]$, then $m'=(X-\gamma)(2g+(X-\gamma)g')$, so $X-\gamma$ divides $Um+Vm'=1$, impossible. Hence below, and in steps 3-5, separable may be read in either sense. By [lem-sfb-complement-semisimple-minpoly-squarefree], condition (i) implies that $m_T$ is squarefree. Since $k$ is perfect, [lem-sfb-perfect-polynomial-squarefree-separable] makes it separable, proving (ii). Conversely, (ii) makes $m_T$ squarefree by the same polynomial lemma, and $m_T(T)=0$ by its defining property. Apply [lem-sfb-squarefree-annihilator-invariant-complements] with $p=m_T$ to obtain (i). Thus (i) and (ii) are equivalent.

source.place: Section 9b, p.166, minimum-polynomial criterion; invariant-complement comparison uses Mathlib Semisimple.lean:74-76,218-245 and Perfect.lean:327-334.

proof.text: We next prove (ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii) for an arbitrary field $K$, without assuming it perfect. Write $A$ for an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $K$-space and choose an algebraic closure $\Omega/K$. Put $B=1\otimes A$. By [lem-sfb-endomorphism-minpoly-scalar-extension], $\Omega\otimes_K V$ is finite-dimensional and $m_B$ is the coefficient image of $m_A$. If $m_A$ is separable, [lem-sfb-polynomial-separability-field-map] makes $m_B$ separable; [lem-sfb-perfect-polynomial-squarefree-separable], in its implication requiring no perfectness, makes $m_B$ squarefree. It annihilates $B$, so [lem-sfb-squarefree-annihilator-invariant-complements] gives invariant complements for $B$. The algebraically closed field and finite-dimensional hypotheses now allow [lem-sfb-invariant-complements-eigenspace-span], giving a spanning set of $B$-eigenvectors. Choose finitely many of these spanning the finite-dimensional space (expand a finite spanning set as finite sums of eigenvectors), and successively remove any vector depending on the others. The resulting basis consists of eigenvectors. This proves geometric diagonalizability from separability.

source.place: Section 9b, p.166, geometric diagonalizability; supporting comparison over arbitrary K supplied by the agent, using Mathlib eigenspace-span and squarefree-annihilator leaves.

proof.text: Conversely, keep the arbitrary field $K$ and suppose $B$ has an eigenbasis $(e_i)$ over $\Omega$. Let $S$ be the finite set of its distinct eigenvalues and put $Q(X)=\prod_{a\in S}(X-a)$. For every $i$, one factor of $Q(B)e_i$ is zero, so $Q(B)=0$. Divide $Q$ by the monic polynomial $m_B$: $Q=q m_B+r$, $\deg r<\deg m_B$. Evaluating at $B$ gives $r(B)=0$; if $r\ne0$, divide by its leading coefficient to obtain a monic annihilator of smaller degree, a contradiction. Thus $m_B\mid Q$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-distinct-linear-factors-separable] with both fields equal to $\Omega$: the factors of $Q$ are pairwise distinct, so every divisor, in particular $m_B$, is separable. By [lem-sfb-endomorphism-minpoly-scalar-extension], this is the coefficient image of $m_A$, and [lem-sfb-polynomial-separability-field-map] reflects its separability back to $K$. This proves the converse without perfectness. Applied to $K=k$, steps 3-4 prove (ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii), completing the three-way equivalence.

source.place: Section 9b, p.166, diagonal eigenbasis and minimum-polynomial criterion; explicit Euclidean-division argument and arbitrary-field comparison supplied by the agent. Distinct-factor criterion: Stacks 09H3 via the cited existing node.

proof.text: Let $L/k$ be any field extension. By [lem-sfb-endomorphism-minpoly-scalar-extension], $L\otimes_k V$ is finite-dimensional and $m_{T_L}$ is the coefficient image of $m_T$. By [lem-sfb-polynomial-separability-field-map], $m_{T_L}$ is separable if and only if $m_T$ is separable. Steps 3-4, which did not assume a perfect base, identify the first assertion with geometric diagonalizability over $L$ and the second with geometric diagonalizability over $k$. This proves preservation and reflection under arbitrary $L/k$, including imperfect or transcendental $L$, and includes $V=0$ by step 1.
